title: Automated Alarm System
tagline: A home alarm my dad and I hacked together in 2020, and I've rebuilt twice since
summary: This started in 2020, when my dad and I opened up a cheap wireless alarm panel and wired its lights into a Raspberry Pi. Since then it's gone through three versions: the original script, a full-screen Pygame console, and now a web dashboard I can check from my phone.

overview.what: A home alarm system built around a cheap wireless alarm panel and a Raspberry Pi. It started as a script reading the panel's lights and is now a web dashboard I can check from my phone.
overview.why: In 2020 our alarm panel could only light up an LED for each open door. My dad and I wanted it to do a lot more, like send alerts, silence the beeper and keep track of everything.
overview.did: My dad and I wired the panel's lights into a Pi. Then I wrote three versions of the software: the first script, a full-screen Pygame console with no AI help, and a set of small programs with a Flask dashboard.
overview.result: It runs on our home network today. Each rebuild fixed what broke the last one, and it's how I learned about memory that keeps growing and splitting a program into parts.

sections.heading: Version one: reading the lights (2020)
body: The alarm panel had a little light for each door sensor. Instead of replacing it, we soldered wires onto those lights and fed them into a Raspberry Pi, so my program could tell when the garage, gate, back door or front door opened. Some states blink, so the code watches each light for 15 seconds to tell a really open door from a flaky sensor. A relay let the Pi silence the panel's beeper too.

sections.heading: Version two: a Pygame console (2022)
body: In 2022 I turned it into a full-screen control panel in Pygame, without any AI help. Pygame doesn't come with buttons or menus, so I drew every one myself, which basically meant building my own small UI toolkit. It had modes like Home, Night and Away, each with its own alerts and sounds, plus a stats page that counted how often each door opened.

sections.heading: Settings and a hidden mushroom
body: The settings screen had audio, timers, modes, stats, motion and email settings, and some of it was locked behind a PIN. The little mushroom in the corner is a hidden exit button, just for fun.

media.alt: Pygame settings hub with large Audio, Time, Modes, Facts, Motion, Emails and Exit buttons plus a mushroom icon
media.caption: The settings screen.

sections.heading: The crash that changed everything
body: The Pygame version ran all day on a Pi, but after a week or two it would run out of resources and crash. A bug that only shows up after days is really hard to track down. It taught me to think about things like memory that keeps growing, logs that never get cleaned up, and which part of a program owns which data.

sections.heading: Version three: a team of small programs (2025)
body: So in 2025 I rebuilt it as a bunch of small programs that talk to each other: one for the sensors, one for the saved data, one for sound, one for motion sensors, one for cameras, one for Telegram alerts, and a Flask web app on top. I didn't know the word microservices yet. I just kept splitting things up until each part had one job. I used ChatGPT while building this version.

media.alt: Mermaid architecture diagram connecting alarm LEDs, motion nodes, ESP32 cameras and phones to the alarm system's local services, orchestrator, web dashboard and alert providers
media.caption: How the pieces connect.

sections.heading: The web dashboard
body: The dashboard keeps the same four big door tiles, green for closed and red for open, and they update live. There's a facts page, a history page, settings, and an admin page where I approve new devices. It runs on our home network, and I use Tailscale to reach it from anywhere without putting it on the public internet.

media.alt: AlarmSystem facts dashboard showing 418 tracking days, totals, and per-door opening and finicky statistics
media.caption: The facts page, with demo numbers.

sections.heading: What's next
body: The new setup makes it easy to add sensors that don't have to wire back to one Pi, so next I want Wi-Fi motion sensors built from Raspberry Pi Picos and more ESP32 cameras. If I rebuilt the messaging today I'd probably use something like Redis instead of writing it all myself, but writing it myself is how I learned why tools like that exist.

RUNTIME VERIFICATION: The Pygame interface ran from its own Python 3.9.13 / Pygame 2.1.2 environment. Hardware calls are commented in this PC copy, so only the UI was exercised; pygame_settings.webp is a direct framebuffer capture from that run. The current web system was copied into an isolated preview directory without its .env or live data, then Data Server, System Server, Motion Server, Camera Hub, Audio Server, and Flask app were run locally with fictional fixtures. Browser checks covered sensor cards and live updates, motion, cameras, facts, event history, General/Security/Telegram settings, and Admin Overview/Accounts/Add. No Telegram message, email, real TTS generation, real GPIO operation, VPN connection, or other external side effect was attempted. web_dashboard.webp, web_facts.webp, and web_admin.webp contain only fictional names, RFC 5737 documentation IP addresses, localhost, and synthetic statistics. The motion ingest accepted two authenticated test triggers and exposed an active session with its idle deadline; the camera hub accepted eight generated JPEG frames, reported 8.78 FPS, and returned an MJPEG stream containing JPEG data. Audio endpoints were tested without an external API call: empty TTS was a no-op success, missing and unknown sound keys returned the expected validation errors. Existing Data Server tests passed 5/5 including concurrent access and 1,000 writes; Relay Server tests passed 6/6. The repository's System Server test file is stale and fails during import because it expects SENSOR_ORDER and older constructor/method names. A direct current-API probe confirmed the change queue remains capped at 10,000 entries but also found that the unmodified simulator reports initial/open/closed sensor choices as open after they pass through the legacy decoder; the portfolio screenshot therefore used a temporary simulator-only logical-state override in the isolated copy. LONG-RUNTIME FAILURE HONESTY: The author remembers the Pygame system failing after roughly one or two weeks and believes an ever-growing state list caused it. No persistent unbounded sensor/status append exists in this surviving snapshot: make_lists creates four fixed entries and get_led creates a fresh local list per poll. The snapshot does show an uncapped main loop because fpsClock.tick(fps) is commented out, plus repeated whole-file reads in the hot path and queued/logged disk I/O. Those are verified resource-pressure risks, but the precise historical memory leak was not reproduced or proven. The public copy therefore distinguishes the observed long-runtime crash, the author's recollection, and what this archived source actually establishes. architecture.webp is a code-derived diagram; the Hardware Server is marked as an unfinished prototype because it is present in source, not launched by main.py, and shares default port 9103 with Motion Server.
